chunks: Dielectric losses and their mechanisms. The question: Explain any dielectric losses and how they occur.
A dielectric is an insulator that sits between the plates of a capacitor, or inside a circuit-board laminate. An ideal one stores energy and gives it all back.
A real one wastes a little as heat. That waste is dielectric loss.
It comes from small leakage current, and mostly from charges inside the material that cannot keep up when the field flips back and forth.
Picture pushing a child on a swing through thick mud. A bit of the effort is stored in the swing's motion, but some is lost to friction in the mud every cycle.
A dielectric is similar: the field twists molecules back and forth, and they rub against their neighbors, producing heat. Faster flipping means more twists per second.
The analogy breaks down at very high frequency, where molecules cannot follow at all.
Phasor view of a lossy capacitor. The current no longer leads the voltage by a full 90°; it's short by the loss angle δ.
The small in-phase component times the voltage is the dissipated power. For C0G, δ is under 0. 06°; for standard FR-4 at GHz, about 1°.
Dielectric: an insulating material that stores energy in an electric field. Polarization: charges in the material shifting or turning in response to a field.
Leakage current: a tiny current that flows through a nonperfect insulator. Loss tangent ( delta ): the power turned into heat as a fraction of the power sloshing in and out.
Smaller is better. Capacitor: two conductors separated by a dielectric, which store charge.
Put 10 volts at 1 kilohertz across a 1 microfarads capacitor. Energy sloshes into and out of the capacitor every cycle.
That flow, called reactive power, is V squared omega C , where omega equals 2 pi f : here 100 times 6. 28 times 10 to the -3 about 0.
63 VA (volt-amperes, watt-like units for power that is not used up). If the loss tangent is 0. 01, the heat is 1% of that, about 6 milliwatts. With a poorer dielectric at 0.
1, it is about 63 milliwatts. That is the whole idea.
"Real dielectrics turn some AC field energy into heat.

Mechanisms: leakage conduction, mainly at low frequency; polarization lag, where dipoles and ions can't reorient fast enough and lose energy to the lattice, peaking near the relaxation frequency; interfacial charge in composites; hysteresis in ferroelectric ceramics like X7R; and partial discharge at high voltage.
We quantify it with the loss tangent: P equals V squared omega C delta . That's why C0G and film caps are used in resonant circuits and low-Df laminates for high-speed boards."
